flashcards.definition: Computers connected by cabling and switches at one site, such as a floor, a building, or a campus of nearby buildings, usually owned by the organization that uses it.
A network that spans multiple geographic locations, such as branch offices linked to a head office using cabling leased from an ISP; the Internet is one example.
A local network that uses radios and antennas to send and receive data, mostly based on the IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) standards; it is often a segment of the same LAN as wired Ethernet.
A network covering an area about the size of a city, such as one company's connected networks within that city; larger than a LAN but smaller than a WAN.
Wireless connections to devices within a few meters; the most common example is Bluetooth earbuds and a smartwatch connected to one person's phone.
A dedicated high-speed network, separate from the LAN, that joins storage such as RAID arrays and tape drives so servers can use it as if it were directly attached.
The unique hardware (physical) address of each Ethernet NIC port: 48 bits, usually written as 12 hexadecimal digits, with the first 24 bits identifying the manufacturer.
The panel where cables from the wall ports end in punchdown blocks on the back; patch cords connect its front RJ45 ports to switch ports, making connections easy to change.
Connects multiple devices in a network with one port per device, forwarding each frame to the port that matches its destination MAC address in its MAC address table.
A switch that needs no configuration and works as soon as it is powered on with hosts connected; common ones have four or eight ports for small networks.
A switch for larger networks that an administrator can connect to over a management port to configure security settings and advanced features, using a web or command line interface.
Supplies electrical power over ordinary Ethernet data cabling to powered devices such as VoIP phones, cameras, and wireless access points.
The PoE standard that supplies up to 15.4 W, about 13 W usable at the device, enough for basic VoIP handsets, wireless access points, and security cameras.
The PoE standard that lets a device draw up to about 25 W, for devices that need more power, such as advanced access points, pan-tilt-zoom cameras, and video IP phones.
The PoE standard that supplies up to about 51 W (Type 3) or 73 W (Type 4) of usable power, for high-power devices such as LED lighting, digital signage, and point-of-sale systems.
A switch that supplies power through its ports; it first detects whether each connected device is PoE enabled and sends no power to one that is not, so it causes no damage.
A device that adds power when a switch does not support PoE; one port connects to the switch port and the other to the powered device, with no more than 100 m of cable overall.
The most popular network cable: four copper wire pairs with no shielding, each pair twisted at a different rate to reduce interference, with a recommended maximum of 100 m (328 feet) per segment.
Twisted pair cable with foil or braided shielding for extra protection against interference; typically required near fluorescent lights, power lines, motors, or generators.
Twisted pair cable for 100 Mbps Fast Ethernet up to 100 m; it is no longer sold, and a network cabled with it will probably need rewiring for Gigabit Ethernet.
Twisted pair cable for 1 Gbps (Gigabit Ethernet) up to 100 m; still acceptable for client computers, though most sites now install Cat 6 instead.
Twisted pair cable for 1 Gbps up to 100 m, more reliable than Cat 5e for Gigabit Ethernet, that also supports 10 Gbps but only up to 55 m (180 feet).
Twisted pair cable for 10 Gbps over the full 100 m; bulkier and heavier than Cat 6, and recommended for 802.3bt PoE and cable runs to wireless access points.
Twisted pair cable for 10 Gbps up to 100 m or 100 Gbps up to 15 m (50 feet); not widely used yet outside short, high-bandwidth runs such as in data centers.
Twisted pair cable for 25 or 40 Gbps up to 30 m (100 feet); used mainly in short, high-bandwidth runs such as in data centers, not in typical home or office networks.
The modular connector that terminates four-pair twisted pair Ethernet cable; also called 8P8C, for eight-position/eight-contact.
The twisted pair wiring standard that puts the green pair on pins 1 and 2 (green/white on pin 1) and the orange pair on pins 3 and 6.
The twisted pair wiring standard that puts the orange pair on pins 1 and 2 (orange/white on pin 1) and the green pair on pins 3 and 6.
The connector typically used on two-pair twisted pair cable, as in telephone systems and broadband DSL modems.
An insulation displacement connector (IDC) where permanent cable is terminated at wall ports and on the back of patch panels; blades in its terminals cut through each wire's insulation.
A tool that scores a cable's outer jacket just enough to remove it, exposing the wire pairs without damaging their insulation, before the cable is terminated.
A tool that presses each wire into the color-coded terminals of an IDC (punchdown block) at a wall port or patch panel.
A tool that attaches an RJ45 plug to the end of a patch cord, piercing the wire insulation at the pins and sealing the plug to the cable jacket.
A pair of devices attached to each end of a cable that energize each wire in turn, with LEDs showing whether every wire conducts and reaches the same pin at both ends.
A tone generator that puts a continuous audio signal on a cable and a probe that detects it, used to trace a cable or pick it out of a bundle when it is not labeled.
An adapter that plugs into a NIC or switch port to test it; a solid link LED shows that the port can send and receive.
A device that intercepts the signals passing over a cable and sends them to a packet or protocol analyzer; passive taps need no power, while active taps are powered.
Fire-retardant cable required in plenum spaces, such as false ceilings that carry HVAC systems; it must give off little smoke when burned, and its jacket is marked CMP.
Outdoor cable that is laid and then covered with earth or concrete; it is often gel-filled against damp and temperature extremes and may be armored against rodents.
Cable that carries light pulses through a glass core; unlike copper, it is not affected by interference and loses less signal over distance, so it supports faster, longer runs.
Fiber with a small core that carries a laser signal, supporting high data rates over runs of many kilometers; it costs more to deploy than multimode.
Fiber with a larger core and cheaper light sources such as LEDs; it costs less than single-mode but supports lower speeds and shorter distances, so it suits LANs more than WANs.
A bayonet-style fiber optic connector with a push-and-twist lock, used mostly on older multimode networks.
A push/pull fiber optic connector, larger than LC, that is simple to insert and remove; it works with single-mode or multimode fiber in simplex or duplex versions.
A small form factor fiber optic connector with a tabbed push/pull design; similar to SC but smaller, so more ports fit in the same space.
Copper cable with a core signal conductor and a wire mesh conductor sharing the same axis, the mesh acting as shielding and ground; used for CCTV, cable TV, and cable modems.
The screw-down connector that typically terminates coax for cable TV (CATV), such as the patch cable to a broadband cable modem.
The device wireless clients connect through, acting as a bridge to the wired network; it is cabled to a switch like a host computer and is often powered by PoE.
One of the smaller frequency ranges a wireless band is split into; channels act like lanes so nearby networks can share a band without interfering.
The size of each Wi-Fi channel, such as 20 or 40 MHz; bonding channels together makes a wider channel, and the wider the channel, the more data it can carry.
The Wi-Fi band that passes through walls best, giving the longest range, but it has few channels and is crowded by other networks, Bluetooth, and microwave ovens.
The Wi-Fi band with more channels and less congestion and interference than 2.4 GHz, giving higher data rates, and a range shorter than 2.4 GHz but longer than 6 GHz.
The newest Wi-Fi band: much faster and less congested than 2.4 and 5 GHz, but it passes through walls the least, so it has the shortest range.
The Wi-Fi standard that uses only the 5 GHz band, with a maximum data rate of 54 Mbps over 20 MHz channels.
The Wi-Fi standard that uses the 2.4 GHz band at a nominal data rate of just 11 Mbps, with 22 MHz channels that overlap heavily.
Channels 1, 6, and 11, the only three 2.4 GHz channels that do not overlap; access points whose ranges overlap should use them to avoid interference.
The Wi-Fi standard that runs at up to 54 Mbps in the 2.4 GHz band, with devices that can also support older 802.11b clients.
The Wi-Fi standard that works in both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz and added channel bonding (40 MHz channels) and MIMO, which uses multiple antennas, for more bandwidth.
The Wi-Fi standard that works only in the 5 GHz band, with 80 and 160 MHz bonded channels and downlink MU-MIMO to send to up to four clients at once.
The Wi-Fi standard that works in both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, reaches 600 Mbps per stream, and supports up to eight clients at once for better performance in congested areas.
The standard that adds the 6 GHz band to Wi-Fi 6; that band has less range but more frequency space, making 80 and 160 MHz channels easier to use.
The Wi-Fi standard that uses the 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz bands, with 320 MHz channels in 6 GHz for speeds up to 46 Gbps and Multi-Link Operation (MLO) across bands.
Hardware or software, such as an app on a laptop or phone, that measures the signal strength of nearby networks on each channel to plan channels and troubleshoot Wi-Fi.
A wireless PAN technology that connects peripherals such as headphones, speakers, and wearables to PCs and phones; devices pair to authenticate and exchange data securely.
Identifies and tracks objects with encoded tags, passive (unpowered) or active (powered), that answer a reader's scan; used in parcel labels and access badges for electronic locks.
A very short-range, peer-to-peer version of RFID in which a device can act as both tag and reader; used for contactless payments, security ID tags, and pairing Bluetooth devices.
